Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo gentleman with a history of Hep C cirrhosis, now admitted 
for increasing abdominal girth and hematuria. 

# Increasing Abdominal Girth/Cirrhosis: The patient has noted an 
increase in the size of his abdomen over the past two weeks; he 
had recently seen his hepatologist who had started him on 
Furosemide 40 mg QOD, in addition to the 25 mg of Spironolactone 
he was taking daily. On admission, patient noted to have ascites 
on U/S, but no evidence of PVT. The patient also denied any 
hematemesis or hematochezia/melena, and this was confirmed with 
a guaiac negative stool. A paracentesis performed under 
ultrasound did not reveal any evidence of SBP. That paracentesis 
removed 2.5 L of fluid, and he was subsequently given albumin 
for replacement. His Furosemide dose was increased to 40 mg 
Daily to be taken simultaneously with a larger dose of his 
Spironolactone at 100 mg Daily. He was not treated for SBP, and 
nutrition was consulted in order to provide information 
regarding a low salt diet. 

# Hepatitis C Cirrhosis: The patient had good virologic response 
to his treatment with Ribavirin, interferon, and filgrastim, 
with less than 43 IU/mL copies on ___. However, given 
that the patient's platelet count on discharge was 44, it was 
felt to be too risky to continue HCV therapy, and the patient's 
Ribavirin, interferon, and filgrastim were discontinued on his 
discharge, with plans to follow-up with his hepatologist for 
further HCV management.

# Hematuria: The patient's hematuria cleared during admission, 
and a U/A prior to his discharge did not show any evidence of 
blood either. His hematuria was felt likely secondary to a very 
small stone or urinary grit which may have traumatized in the 
urinary system; because of his very low platelet count, this 
likely resulted in his hematuria. The patient's wife works with 
a urologist, and the patient has plans to follow-up with urology 
for possible cystoscopy in the setting of hematuria.

# Abdominal Pain pain: The intermittent nature and sharp 
character of the patient's pain at OSH was not consistent with 
SBP, and the patient's pain resolved with Dilaudid at OSH, and 
did not require additional pain medication on admission. His U/S 
did show cholelithiasis, but there was no active sign of 
obstruction, and the patient's alk phos was within normal 
limits. Surgical consult was deferred given the patient's 
possibility of transplantation in the future, and the fact that 
the patient was not currently having symptoms consistent with 
cholecystitis on admission.

Discharge Instructions:
Mr. ___, it was a pleasure taking care of you in the 
hospital. You were transferred to ___ because of concerns 
regarding the increasing amount of abdominal girth you've 
noticed, in addition to the fact that you've noted blood in your 
urine.

We performed several tests on you while you were in the 
hospital; an ultrasound of your abdomen showed fluid, no clot in 
your portal ___, but did show some stones in your gallbladder. 

We also took some fluid off of your abdomen using a needle to 
see if you had an infection in your abdomen.  The fluid showed 
no evidence of this.  You had 2.5L of fluid removed to help with 
your symptoms of increased abdominal girth.  The dose of your 
diuretics have been increased to help remove some of this fluid. 
 You will also need to adhere to a very strict low salt diet to 
keep the fluid off.  This means NO canned soups/vegetables, 
prepared TV dinners, take-out ___ food, processed meats, 
chips or other junk foods high in salt.  In general, fresh 
fruits and vegetables and home-cooked food is acceptable.  

Your urine started to clear up as you were admitted to the 
hospital. We felt that the blood in your urine likely due to the 
fact that you have low platelets, probably from a combination of 
your liver disease and the medications which you are taking for 
Hepatitis C. When you had left the hospital, you felt as thought 
your urine had started to clear up.  You should see a urologist 
after you leave the hospital to follow this up.

Because of your low platelet count, it is too dangerous for you 
to continue to take your medications for Hepatitis C. We 
discontinued all of these medications upon your admission to the 
hospital.  You may be able to restart these medications later 
should your liver function improve; you should discuss this with 
Dr. ___.

When you leave the hospital:
- CHANGE your dose of Furosemide to 40 mg Daily (previously you 
had been taking 40 mg every other day)
- CHANGE your dose of Spironolactone to 100 mg Daily (previously 
you had been taking 25 mg Daily)
- STOP taking peginterferon alfa 2a 180 mcg every ___ 
- STOP taking ribavirin 600 mg twice a day
- STOP taking filgrastim 300 mcg every ___

We did not make any other changes to your medications, so please 
continue to take them as you normally have been.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ man with hepatitis C cirrhosis, presents with several
weeks of increasing abdominal distention and hematuria.  Please evaluate for
portal vein thrombosis, gallstones or other acute process.

TECHNIQUE:  Gray scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the liver and
gallbladder were obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT of the outside hospital from ___ and CTA of the
abdomen from ___.

FINDINGS:  The liver is severely cirrhotic without focal lesions.  The portal
vein is patent with normal hepatopetal flow.  There is no intra- or
extra-hepatic biliary dilatation with the common bile duct measuring 4 mm. 
The hepatic veins are patent.  There is large amount of ascites.  The spleen
is enlarged measuring 17 cm.  The gallbladder is collapsed with a thickened
wall due to edema consistent with the associated ascites.  Multiple gallstones
are seen, but there is no evidence of cholecystitis.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Patent portal and hepatic veins.
2.  Cholelithiasis, but no evidence of cholecystitis.
3.  Large amount of ascites.

INDICATION:  ___ male with HCV cirrhosis and new ascites.  Evaluate
for SBP.

OPERATOR:  ___, M.D., attending; ___, M.D., resident.
 
PROCEDURE:  Following discussion of the risks and benefits of the procedure,
written informed consent was obtained from the patient.  A preprocedure
timeout was performed verifying three patient identifiers and the procedure to
be performed. Under ultrasound guidance, a pocket of ascites in the right
lower quadrant was located.  The patient was prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.  Local anesthesia was provided with subcutaneous injection of
1% buffered lidocaine.  Initial attempt to place a ___ ___ catheter into
the peritoneal cavity was unsuccessful due to insufficient length. A longer
10-cm ___ ___ catheter was subsequently successfully introduced into the
peritoneal cavity.  Approximately 20 cc of clear yellow-green peritoneal fluid
was aspirated and sent to the lab for analysis.  Subsequently, approximately
2.5 liters of peritoneal fluid was aspirated.  One liter of this aspirate was
sent for laboratory analysis as requested by the clinical team.  The catheter
was removed and hemostasis was achieved with direct pressure.  The wound was
dressed.  There were no immediate complications. The attending radiologist,
Dr. ___, was present and supervising throughout, and performed portions of,
the procedure.

IMPRESSION:  Technically successful US guided diagnostic and therapeutic
paracentesis.
